IN RE: MARK F MILLER JR
PETITION FOR Review for Personal Income Tax
PERIOD(S) 2011
AND NOW, May 20, 2014, pursuant to the Fiscal Code, the Act of 1929, April 9, P.L. 343,
as amended, (72 P.S. § 1 et seq), the Board of Finance and Revenue of the Commonwealth of
Pennsylvania, based upon the reasons set forth herein, hereby ORDERS the following:
Jurisdiction
This petition comes before the Board of Finance and Revenue pursuant to Section 2704
of the Tax Reform Code, as amended, 72 P.S. § 9704.
Issue
Whether Petitioner has established that the Department improperly disallowed his
claimed Schedule UE expenses.
Statement of the Case
Petitioner, Mark F. Miller Jr., timely filed his 2011 Form PA-40, reporting $ of
gross compensation and deducting $ in Schedule UE expenses for a net compensation
of $ . Petitioner reported $ of taxable income and a tax liability of $ .
The Department reviewed the return and determined that Petitioner’s Schedule UE
expenses were excessive in relation to his compensation, and disallowed all claimed
expenses. The Department increased his tax liability to $ , and issued an assessment
notice for the additional tax due, plus penalties and interest.
Petitioner appealed the assessment notice to the Board of Appeals (“BOA”) on May 3,
2013, claiming that all of the expenses were correct as originally filed. In its Decision and
Order dated October 1, 2013, the BOA denied the petition, finding that the mileage and other
travel expenses should be classified as commuting miles, which are not deductible, and that

the meals and entertainment expenses claimed are not ordinary, reasonable, and actually
incurred in performing the duties of the job.
Petitioner files the instant matter at the Board of Finance and Revenue raising the same
claims as raised at the BOA. Petitioner avers he was an insurance sales representative and in
the course of his duties he was required to use his vehicle, cellphone, and incur other costs
that were not reimbursed by his employer. Petitioner states he was compensated through
commissions only, and the expenses incurred in his travel were reasonable and necessary in
order to earn such commissions. Petitioner also argues that it was customary in his profession
to provide periodic meals and entertainment for purposes of representing his products and
securing subsequent sales. Petitioner argues that while the Department may consider these
expenses to be excessive in comparison to his income, it should be noted that he was a recent
college graduate and was newly learning the intricacies of the position while incurring these
expenses.
Petitioner has submitted a letter from Northwestern Mutual Financial Network verifying
that he was a statutory employee responsible for any expenses incurred in the generation of
income.
In a letter mailed March 11, 2014, Board Counsel requested that Petitioner provide a
mileage log detailing the dates and locations traveled and the business purpose, along with
receipts, invoices, and other verification of the expenses claimed. As of this date, no further
evidence has been submitted.
Statement of the Law
An employee who is required, as a condition of her employment, to pay all her
expenses and who is not reimbursed separately for these expenses is permitted to exclude
from income the amount to be paid for legitimate business expenses. See Commonwealth v.
Staley, 476 Pa. 171, 381 A.2d 1280 (1978); Ritz v. Commonwealth, 495 Pa. 1, 432 A.2d 169
(1981).
Legitimate business expenses are those which are ordinary, actual, reasonable and
necessary to the business conducted. See Ritz 495 Pa. 1, 6, 432 A.2d 169 (1981).
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.
72 P.S. § 9705.
Conclusion
Petitioner’s request for relief is denied. Legitimate business expenses are those which
are ordinary, actual, reasonable and necessary to the business conducted. See Ritz 495 Pa.
1, 6, 432 A.2d 169 (1981). While Petitioner has established that he was expected to incur
costs in the course of his employment for which he was not reimbursed, he has not provided
the requested evidence verifying those expenses. Petitioner has failed to meet his burden of
proof imposed by 72 P.S. § 9705.

Jurisdiction
This petition comes before the Board of Finance and Revenue pursuant to Section 2704
of the Tax Reform Code of 1971, as amended, 72 P.S. § 9704.
Issue
Whether a Petition for Reassessment was timely filed with the Board of Appeals.
Statement of the Case
Petitioners, Thomas and Mary Peduzzi, originally filed their 2003 Form PA-40 reporting
a tax liability of $ . For the net profits class of income Petitioners reported a loss of
$( ) resulting largely from Petitioners’ interest in Fund LLC (“ ”), which
passed through a loss of $( ) to Petitioners. The Department reviewed the return and
disallowed the loss reported by because it had not filed an information return with the
Department. As a result of the adjustments, the Department increased Petitioners’ tax liability
to $ and issued an assessment notice on December 5, 2006, for the additional tax due
plus penalties and interest.
The Board of Appeals (“BOA”) received a Petition for Reassessment on August 13,
2013. In its Decision and Order dated August 26, 2013, the BOA dismissed the petitions for

Petitioners file the instant matter at the Board of Finance and Revenue arguing that the
Department improperly disallowed the loss pass through by .

In a letter mailed December 11, 2013, Board Counsel informed Petitioner of the
jurisdictional defect. Petitioner argued at hearing that he supplied his accountant with the
assessment and assumed that the accountant was handling any appeal. The Board has no
record of any timely appeal.
Statement of the Law
Section 340 of the Tax Reform Code of 1971 states in part: “Any taxpayer against
whom an assessment is made may petition the department for a reassessment pursuant to
Article XXVII.” 72 P.S. § 7340.
General rule.--A taxpayer may file a petition for reassessment with the department
within 90 days after the mailing date of the notice of assessment. 72 P.S. § 9702(a).
Our Supreme Court has held that limitations periods are absolute conditions to a right to
obtain relief. Federal Deposits Ins. Corp. v. Board of Finance and Revenue, 368 Pa. 463, 469-
470; 84 A.2d 495, 498-499 (1951). In any case, equitable principles cannot vary the statutory
time requirements. See Bethlehem Steel Co. v. Board of Finance and Revenue, 431 Pa. 1,
10; 244 A.2d 767, 772 (1968) and Cooper v. Commonwealth, 700 A.2d 553, 554-555 (Pa.
Commw. 1997).
Conclusion
Petitioners filed the Petition for Reassessment at the Board of Appeals beyond the
ninety day filing period. Petitioners failed to provide adequate evidence to overcome the
jurisdiction issue. Therefore, the Board of Appeals properly dismissed Petitioners’ claim for
failure to file a timely appeal of the assessment. See 72 P.S. § 9702(a).
Accordingly, this Board enters the following:
ORDER
This petition is dismissed.

AND NOW, May 20, 2014, pursuant to the Fiscal Code, the Act of 1929, April 9, P.L. 343,

Pennsylvania, based upon the reasons set forth herein, hereby ORDERS the following:
Jurisdiction
This petition comes before the Board of Finance and Revenue pursuant to Section 2704
of the Tax Reform Code of 1971, as amended, 72 P.S. § 9704.
Issue
Whether Petitioners were improperly assessed tax, penalties and interest on income
earned in New Jersey.
Statement of the Case
Petitioners, John L. and Vonetta Smith Jr., file the instant matter at the Board of Finance
and Revenue claiming that the tax which they were assessed by the Department of Revenue
for the 2008 tax year was withheld to New Jersey by Mr. Smith’s employer. Petitioners were
Pennsylvania residents earning income in New Jersey. The Department assessed Petitioners
on $ of compensation, and a tax liability of $ . The Department issued an
assessment notice on December 11, 2009, for the outstanding tax, plus penalties and interest.
Petitioners filed an appeal at the Board of Appeals (“BOA”) claiming that the
assessment was made in error because Mr. Smith had paid tax through his employer’s
withholding to New Jersey. In its Decision and Order dated November 21, 2013, the BOA
denied the petition, finding that Petitioners had not submitted evidence to support their appeal.
Petitioners file the instant matter at the Board of Finance and Revenue arguing that they
should not be penalized for Mr. Smith’s employer’s failure to properly withhold tax to
Mailed: JOHN L & VONETTA SMITH JR on May 23, 2014

JOHN L & VONETTA SMITH JR BF&R Docket No.: 1319177
Pennsylvania in accordance with the reciprocal agreement between New Jersey and
Pennsylvania. Petitioners states that Mr. Smith requested that his employer withhold
Pennsylvania taxes, but that his request was refused. Department records show that
Petitioners had a total of $ of taxes withheld to New Jersey from their compensation.
Statement of the Law
Pennsylvania has entered into reciprocal agreements with Indiana, Maryland, New
Jersey, Ohio, Virginia, and West Virginia. Personal Income Tax Guide, 7-15 (Revised
February 2007), see also, Pa. Dept. of Revenue Ltr. Rul. PIT-05-016 (July 26, 2005).
Pennsylvania residents must have Pennsylvania taxes withheld on compensation, subject to
federal withholding, earned in reciprocal agreement states. Id. Residents of the reciprocal
agreement states working in Pennsylvania must have their home state’s taxes withheld on
compensation, subject to federal withholding, earned in Pennsylvania. Id.
Upon the filing of a petition for reassessment or a petition for refund as provided under
this act by a taxpayer, additions or penalties imposed upon the taxpayer by the laws of this
Commonwealth may be waived or abated, in whole or in part, where the petitioner has
established that he has acted in good faith, without negligence and with no intent to defraud.
72 P.S. § 9706.
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.
72 P.S. § 9705.
Conclusion
Petitioners’ request for relief is granted in part.
Petitioners’ request to abate the assessed tax is denied. Pennsylvania residents must
have Pennsylvania taxes withheld on compensation, subject to federal withholding, earned in
reciprocal agreement states. Personal Income Tax Guide, 7-15 (Revised February 2007).
Petitioners are Pennsylvania residents working in New Jersey. Their Forms W-2 show that
taxes were withheld to New Jersey, instead of Pennsylvania as required by the reciprocal
agreement between the states. Petitioners have not provided sufficient evidence to establish
that the Department’s assessment was in error.
Petitioners’ request to abate penalties is granted. Penalties imposed upon the taxpayer
by the laws of this Commonwealth may be waived or abated, in whole or in part, where the
petitioner has established that he has acted in good faith, without negligence and with no intent
to defraud. 72 P.S. § 9706. Petitioners have established that they acted in good faith by
requesting Mr. Smith’s employer withhold his taxes to Pennsylvania. The fact that this request
was refused does not disqualify Petitioners from penalty abatement.
Interest is charged to compensate the Commonwealth for the loss of the use of the
funds while the tax shown to have been properly due is in the possession of the taxpayer.
Therefore, Petitioners’ request for abatement of interest must be denied for 2008.

Petitioner protested the assessment notice at the Board of Appeals (”BOA”) claiming
that he and his spouse were domiciled in Florida as of March 10, 2010, and, as such, were no
longer resident individuals of the Commonwealth. By letter and e-mail dated October 18,
2013, the BOA requested that Petitioner’s representative submit a properly completed power
of attorney form in order to perfect the appeal. The correspondence requested that Petitioner’s
representative provide the form within 15 days of the date of the correspondence. By Decision
and Order dated December 19, 2013, the BOA denied Petitioner’s appeal for failure to provide
the power of attorney form.
Petitioner files the instant matter at the Board of Finance and Revenue protesting the
BOA’s Decision and Order. In the appeal filed with this Board, Petitioner’s representative
states that he provided the BOA with documentation to support Petitioner’s claim that he and
his spouse were not domiciled in Pennsylvania during 2010, including legal principals,
arguments, and eight exhibits.
In the appeal filed at the BOA, Petitioner claimed that Florida was his state of domicile
during 2011, because he and his spouse established Florida as their domicile and base of
operations beginning in March 2010. Petitioner stated that a taxpayer's domicile is the state in
which the taxpayer maintains his or her permanent place of abode, and is the place where he
or she intends to return whenever absent. Further, Petitioner stated that when a taxpayer
maintains multiple “permanent abodes,” his domicile is the place where the taxpayer has the
greatest connections and the place which the taxpayer intends to be his or her domicile.
Petitioner stated that an abode is not permanent if it is occupied “only during a fixed or limited
period of time for a particular purpose.” Petitioner asserted that when determining domicile,
the Department was required to consider where the taxpayer spends the greatest amount of
his or her time, where the taxpayer purchases the necessities of life, maintains expensive
furniture or works of art, maintains a driver's license, registers vehicles, maintains hunting or
fishing licenses, carries insurance policies, registers to vote, and files federal income tax
returns.
Petitioner argued that he and his spouse purchased their home in Florida in March
2010, at which time, they transported family photos, works of art, and the necessities of daily
life to the Florida home. Petitioner also contended that they transferred vehicle registrations to
Florida, obtained Florida driver's licenses, registered to vote in Florida, participated in elections
in Florida, and served on jury duty in Florida. Petitioner states that he and his spouse revoked
their will executed in Pennsylvania in favor of a will executed in Florida. Further, Petitioner
states that he and his spouse have only been present in Pennsylvania for limited periods of
time in order to visit family members who still reside in the state. Petitioner contends that he
and his spouse have been domiciled in Florida since March 2010, and are therefore exempted
from Pennsylvania personal income taxes for all subsequent years.
To support the appeal, Petitioner has submitted the following:
• A spreadsheet reporting the number of days that Petitioner claims to have spent in
different states during 2011. The spreadsheet reports that Petitioner spent 143 days in
Pennsylvania, 129 days in Florida, 53 days in Maryland, and 40 days in Nevada during

Statement of the Law
Every resident individual, estate or trust shall be subject to, and shall pay for the
privilege of receiving each of the classes of income hereinafter enumerated in section 303, a
tax upon each dollar of income received by that resident during that resident's taxable year at
the rate of three and seven hundredths per cent. 72 P.S. § 7302(a).
“Resident Individual” means an individual who is domiciled in this Commonwealth
unless he maintains no permanent place of abode in this Commonwealth and does maintain a
permanent place of abode elsewhere and spends in the aggregate not more than thirty days of
the taxable year in this Commonwealth; or who is not domiciled in this Commonwealth but
maintains a permanent place of the abode in this Commonwealth and spends in the aggregate
more than one hundred eighty-three days of taxable year in this Commonwealth.
72 P.S. § 7301(p).
Domicile—The place which an individual intends to be his permanent home and to
which he intends to return whenever he may be absent. 61 Pa. Code § 101.1.
A domicile, once established, continues until the individual in question moves to a new
location with the bona fide intention of making his fixed and permanent home there. No
change of domicile results from a removal to a new location if the intention is to remain there
only for a limited time; this rule applies even though the individual may have sold or disposed
of his former home. The burden shall be upon the individual asserting a change of domicile to
show that the necessary intention exited. In determining an individual’s intention in this regard,
his declarations shall be given due weight, but they may not be conclusive if they are
contradicted by his conduct. The fact that an individual registers and votes in one place is
important but not necessarily conclusive, especially if the facts indicate that he did this merely
to escape taxation in some other place. 61 Pa. Code § 101.3(b).

Where an individual claims to be a nonresident for any taxable year, the burden shall be
upon him to show that during that he satisfied all there of the requirements set forth in
subsection (a). 61 Pa. Code § 101.4(b).
“Homestead.” A dwelling, including the parcel of land on which the dwelling is located
and the other improvements located on the parcel for which any of the following apply:
(1) The dwelling is primarily used as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person.
The homestead for real property qualifying under this paragraph shall not include the
land on which the dwelling is located if the land is not owned by a person who owns the
dwelling.
(2) The dwelling is a unit in a condominium as the term is defined in 68 Pa.C.S. § 3103
(relating to definitions) and the unit is primarily used as the domicile of a natural person
who is an owner of the unit; or the dwelling is a unit in a cooperative as the term is
defined in 68 Pa.C.S. § 4103 (relating to definitions) and the unit is primarily used as the
domicile of a natural person who is an owner of the unit. The homestead for a unit in a
condominium or a cooperative shall be limited to the assessed value of the unit, which
shall be determined in a manner consistent with the assessment of real property taxes
on those units under 68 Pa.C.S. (relating to real and personal property) or as otherwise
provided by law. If the unit is not separately assessed for real property taxes, the
homestead shall be a pro rata share of the real property.
(3) The dwelling does not qualify under paragraphs (1) and (2) and a portion of the
dwelling is used as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person. The homestead
for real property qualifying under this paragraph shall be the portion of the real property
that is equal to the portion of the dwelling that is used as the domicile of an owner.
53 Pa.C.S.A. § 8401 “Homestead.”
Upon the filing of a petition for reassessment or a petition for refund as provided under
this act by a taxpayer, additions or penalties imposed upon the taxpayer by the laws of this
Commonwealth may be waived or abated, in whole or in part, where the petitioner has
established that he has acted in good faith, without negligence and with no intent to defraud.
72 P.S. § 9706.
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.
72 P.S. § 9705.
Conclusion
Petitioner’s request that this Board determine that he was not a resident individual for
tax purposes is denied because, among other reasons, he maintained a homestead exemption
in the Commonwealth and spent more time in Pennsylvania during 2011 than any other state.
A homestead exemption is only available to a Pennsylvania resident and for that resident’s
permanent primary residence on which property taxes are paid. See 53 Pa.C.S.A. § 8401
cyd Page No. 4 CAL. NO. 7

DAVID KAUFMAN BF&R Docket No.: 1319397
“Homestead.” (defining “homestead,” in part, as a dwelling “primarily used as the domicile of
an owner who is a natural person”).
Resident taxpayers are required to pay personal income tax to the Commonwealth for
the privilege of receiving eight enumerated classes of income. See 72 P.S. § 7302(a)
(imposing personal income tax on residents). The term “resident individual” is defined, in part,
as “an individual who is domiciled in this Commonwealth unless he maintains no permanent
place of abode in this Commonwealth and does maintain a permanent place of abode
elsewhere and spends in the aggregate not more than thirty days of the taxable year in this
Commonwealth.” 72 P.S. § 7301(p). The term “domicile” is defined as “[t]he place which an
individual intends to be his permanent home and to which he intends to return whenever he
may be absent.” 61 Pa. Code § 101.1. Domicile continues until the taxpayer moves to new
location with the bona fide intention of making a fixed and permanent home there. 61 Pa.
Code § 101.3(b). In Hvizdak v. Commonwealth, the Commonwealth Court stated that the
Pennsylvania “Supreme Court stated that ‘a domicile of choice may not be retained by
intention alone.’ It must also be shown by one's conduct.” 50 A.3d 788 (Pa Commw. 2012)
(citing Dorrance's Estate, 309 Pa. 151, 170, 163 A. 303, 309 (1932)), aff’d, 69 A.3d 170 (Pa.
2013).
The Board has determined that Petitioner has not met his burden of establishing that he
relinquished his Pennsylvania residency. Additionally, Petitioner spent the greatest portion of
2011 in the Commonwealth, 143 days of 365 days, further showing that he did not change his
domicile to Florida.
Accordingly, the Board orders the following:
ORDER
This petition is denied.

On November 1, 2012, the Department applied the 2011 overpayment to an assessed
liability on Petitioner’s 2008 tax account.
On November 13, 2012, the Department mailed Petitioner a notice informing him that it
applied his 2011 overpayment to an assessed amount on his 2008 tax account.
On May 10, 2013, Petitioner filed a refund claim at the Board of Appeals (“BOA”)
arguing that the Department improperly applied the 2011 overpayment to his 2008 tax account
by collecting the tax liability less than ninety days after the 2008 assessment notice was
issued.
The BOA denied Petitioner’s refund claim stating that “[i]t is this Board’s opinion the
Department did not error in “offsetting” the 2011 tax year refund against liabilities outstanding
on the prior tax years as this is the standard procedure of the Department.” BOA Decision and
Order, page 2 (dated September 24, 2013).
Petitioner files the instant matter at the Board of Finance and Revenue, again claiming
that the Department improperly used his 2011 overpayment to offset the 2008 assessed
liability while a timely appeal of the 2008 assessment was pending. Petitioner also claims that
the Department improperly disallowed his deduction for IDC.
According to Department records, on April 10, 2012, the Department issued a Notice of
Reopened Assessment regarding Petitioner’s 2008 tax account in the amount of $ .
On July 11, 2012, Petitioner filed a timely appeal of the Notice of Reopened Assessment
(Docket No. 1214623) at the BOA. On September 14, 2012, the BOA issued a Decision and
Order regarding Petitioner’s appeal. On November 1, 2012, the Department applied the 2011
overpayment to the 2008 assessed liability. On December 11, 2012, Petitioner filed a timely
appeal of the BOA’s Decision and Order with this Board of Finance and Revenue. On March
29, 2013, this Board rendered a decision in the appeal of Petitioner’s 2008 tax account. On
April 22, 2013, Petitioner filed a timely appeal of this Board’s decision with the Commonwealth
Court.

Collection upon failure to request reassessment, review or appeal

(1) After ninety days from the date of mailing of a copy of the notice of
assessment, if no petition for reassessment has been filed;

Board of Finance and Revenue upon a petition for review or from the expiration of the

may credit the amount of such overpayment against any liability in respect of the tax

(b) The department is authorized to prescribe regulations providing for the

General rule. The Department, within the applicable period of limitations may credit any
overpayment of tax, including interest thereon, against any outstanding liability for any tax, or
for any interest, additional amount, addition to tax, or assessable penalty, owed by the person
making the overpayment, and the balance, if any, will be refunded to such person by the
Department. 61 Pa. Code § 119.12(a).
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.

of law on which the petitioner relies. Any evidence in support of the petition shall be submitted

Conclusion
Petitioner’s request for relief is granted.
Section 344 of the Tax Reform Code sets forth the timeframe in which the Department
is permitted to collect a tax liability upon a taxpayer’s failure to request reassessment, review,
or appeal of an assessment notice. 72 P.S. § 7344. Section 344(1) prohibits the Department
from collecting a tax within ninety days of the date the assessment notice was mailed. 72 P.S.
§ 344(1). Section 344(2) prohibits the Department from collecting a tax within ninety days of
the mailing date of the BOA’s Decision and Order. 72 P.S. § 344(2). Section 344(3) allows
the Department to collect a tax after this Board renders its decision in a matter and the
taxpayer files an appeal with the Commonwealth Court, or after the taxpayer’s appeal period to
the Commonwealth Court expires. 72 P.S. § 344(3).
The Department inappropriately refused to refund Petitioner’s 2011 overpayment by
improperly using it to offset an assessed amount on his 2008 tax account during the pendency
of the administrative appeals process. Petitioner’s 2008 tax account was assessed on April
10, 2012. Petitioner appealed the 2008 assessment notice to the BOA on July 11, 2012. The
BOA rendered a decision on September 14, 2012, and Petitioner appealed that decision to this
Board on December 11, 2012. The Department applied the 2011 overpayment to the 2008
assessed amount on November 1, 2012, which was during the time that Petitioner was allowed
to appeal the BOA’s decision to this Board – without having to pay the assessed amount. As
such, the Department’s application of the 2011 overpayment to the 2008 assessment was
improper and the overpayment shall be refunded to Petitioner.

liability prior to the administrative appeal period ending. That section of the Pennsylvania
Code permits the Department to use an overpayment from one tax period to offset “any
outstanding liability for any tax, or for any interest, additional amount, addition to tax, or
assessable penalty” that the taxpayers owes. 61 Pa. Code § 119.12(a). Petitioner’s assessed
amount for 2008 was not an “outstanding liability” subject to collection under 61 Pa. Code §
119.12(a) when the Department collected the 2008 amount on November 1, 2012, because
Section 344 of the Tax Reform Code prevents the Department from collecting a tax liability
before the administrative appeals period expires.
The Department did not adjust Petitioner’s reported 2011 net profits and taxable
income. Therefore, it did not disallow any reported IDC and this Board will not address

(Arriero), was assessed as a responsible party pursuant to Section 225 of the Tax Reform
Code of 1971. The assessment consisted of sales taxes totaling $ that were collected,
but not remitted to the Commonwealth for the 12M12. Petitioner was also assessed penalties
and interest for the 10M12-12M12. Arriero is a limited liability company organized in
Pennsylvania and files a Federal Partnership return.
A petition was filed with the Board of Appeals wherein Petitioner requested that the
assessment be stricken in its entirety because he was not a shareholder of Arriero during the
period of assessment. Petitioner submitted a copy of an agreement signed by the three
shareholders indicating transfer of ownership of Arriero to Cesare Heriberto Ayala-Reyes on

that the assessment be stricken in its entirety because he was not a shareholder of Arriero
during the period of assessment.
Department of Revenue records verify that Petitioner is a Virginia resident and filed an
NRK-1 for 2009 reporting income or loss from the company. The Federal partnership returns
Forms K-1 for 2010 and 2011 list Petitioner as a general partner owning a % interest.
Arriero has not filed corporation and partnership returns for 2012.
Statement of the Law
All taxes collected by any person from purchasers in accordance with this article and all
taxes collected by any person from purchasers under color of this article which have not been
properly refunded by such person to the purchaser shall constitute a trust fund for the
Commonwealth, and such trust shall be enforceable against such person, his representatives
and any person (other than a purchaser to whom a refund has been made properly) receiving
any part of such fund without consideration, or knowing that the taxpayer is committing a
breach of trust: Provided, however, That any person receiving payment of a lawful obligation
of the taxpayer from such fund shall be presumed to have received the same in good faith and
without any knowledge of the breach of trust. Any person, other than a taxpayer, against
whom the department makes any claim under this section shall have the same right to petition
and appeal as is given taxpayers by any provisions of this part. 72 P.S. § 7225.
In George W. Brown III, as Individual and as President of Electrical Industries, Inc. v.
Commonwealth, 670 A.2d 1222 at 1225 (Pa. Commw. Ct. 1996), the Court determined that, for
the period when the bank took total control over the taxpayer and the officer had no control
over any financial operations, regardless of the fact that the officer remained on the premises
after the bank took control, the Officer was not liable for sales and withholding taxes. The
Court concluded that the taxpayer was not an active or controlling Officer of the corporation for
the period in which the bank held complete control over the financial operations of the
company. Conversely, the Court held that the taxpayer was liable for sales and withholding
taxes for the period in which he remained active and in control of the general management of
the business, including the financial operations.
In reaching this conclusion, the Court in Brown relied on the case of City of Philadelphia
v. B. Axe Company, 40 Pa. Commw. Ct. 257, 397 A.2d 51 (1979), wherein the Court
determined:
[A] corporation collecting taxes as an agent of a municipality
and failing to pay over such taxes to the municipality is a trustee ex
maleficio, and active and controlling corporate officers are
responsible for the performance of that trust duty by the

OSCAR HERRERA BF&R Docket No.: 1307467
corporation. Where such persons fail to perform that duty, the
individuals are trustees ex maleficio as well as the corporation.
Id. at 261, 397 A.2d at 53.
The court in Axe also identified several factors that it considered important in
determining whether a corporate officer and shareholder was responsible for unpaid
withholding tax: physical presence on the premises at relevant times, ability to hire and fire
employees, review and signing tax documents, signing payroll checks, signing checks for
expenses, obtaining loans, consulting the company’s books, and acting as an administrator
and manager.
Conclusion
Upon review of the facts and evidence presented, this Board finds that Petitioner was a
responsible party for the 10M12-12M12 sales tax obligations of Arriero. The evidence is not
sufficient to prove that Petitioner officially sold or transferred his interest in Arriero during 2012.
Therefore, Petitioner is liable for the trust fund obligations for the periods in question.
ORDER
This petition is denied.

was timely filed within three years of the extended filing date and within six months of an audit
assessment.
Petitioner reasons that an appeal period could not have started running without a return
filed. Petitioner did not file until October 15, 2010, and the August 12, 2013 Board of Appeals
filing date was within three years of the extended return filing and timely under 72 P.S. §
10003.1(a).
Petitioner claims that it timely filed for refund at the Board of Appeals on August 12,
2013, which was within six months of the May 15, 2013 audit assessment notice and timely
under 72 P.S. § 10003.1(b).
Petitioner adds that the refund claims were filed to preserve issues not listed on the

Statement of the Law
Our Supreme Court has held that limitations periods are absolute conditions to a right to
obtain relief. Federal Deposit Ins. Corp. v. Board of Finance and Revenue, 368 Pa. 463, 469-
470, 84 A.2d 495, 498-499 (1951). In any case, equitable principles cannot vary the statutory
time requirements. See, e.g., Bethlehem Steel Co. v. Board of Finance and Revenue, 431 Pa.
1, 10, 244 A.2d 767, 772 (1968) and Cooper v. Commonwealth, 700 A.2d 553, 554-555 (Pa.
Commw. 1997).
For a tax collected by the Department of Revenue, a taxpayer who has actually paid
tax, interest or penalty to the Commonwealth or to an agent or licensee of the Commonwealth
authorized to collect taxes may petition the Department of Revenue for refund or credit of the
tax, interest or penalty. Except as otherwise provided by statute, a petition for refund must be
made to the department within three years of actual payment of the tax, interest or penalty.
72 P.S. § 10003.1(a).
The department may grant a refund or credit to a taxpayer for all tax periods covered by
departmental audit. If a credit is not granted by the department in the audit report, the
taxpayer must file a petition for refund for taxes paid with respect to the audit period within six
months of the mailing date of the notice of assessment, determination or settlement or within
three years of actual payment of the tax, whichever is later. 72 P.S. § 10003.1(b).
In the case of amounts paid as a result of an assessment, determination, settlement or
appraisement, a petition for refund must be filed with the department within six months of the
actual payment of the tax. 72 P.S. § 10003.1(d).
A taxpayer shall be deemed to have timely filed a petition for resettlement, a petition for
reassessment, a petition for redetermination or any other protest relating to the assessment of
tax or any other matter relating to any tax imposed by this act if the letter transmitting the
petition is received by the Department of Revenue or is postmarked by the United States

72 P.S. § 10003.6.
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.
72 P.S. § 9705.
Every petition . . . filed with the Board shall set forth the facts and points of law on which
the Petitioner relies. Any evidence in support of the petition shall be submitted simultaneously
with the petition or as promptly as possible thereafter. All evidential material shall be
submitted prior to five working days of the hearing date. 61 Pa. Code § 701.3(c).
Conclusion
The BOA correctly dismissed a refund case filed with a debit balance for the audited
and assessed tax in the tax account, but this refund was also filed more than three years after
the tax payment date.
The BOA only has jurisdiction to decide the merits of those refund cases concerning
money paid to the Commonwealth and filed within three years of the actual payment date or
within six months of an audit assessment. See 72 P.S. § 10003.1(a) and (b). The wording of
the statutes require refund claim amounts to have been paid as well as filing within the
prescribed deadlines. The three year provision in 72 P.S. § 10003.1(a) applies to “. . . a tax
collected by the Department of Revenue, a taxpayer who has actually paid tax,” which
indicates that payment is a requirement for a refund filing. Similarly, 72 P.S. § 10003.1(b)
refers to “filing claims for taxes paid with respect to the audit period,” which also indicates tax
payment is required for a refund claim.
A debit tax balance in Petitioner’s account without payment of that tax balance indicates
that Petitioner did not meet the threshold requirement of a refund claim—that the refund must
concern amounts paid to the Commonwealth. Not only did Petitioner not pay the tax balance
at the time of filing, but the claim was filed late.
Although Petitioner filed for refund within six months of the audit assessment, Petitioner
never paid any portion of the assessed tax and failed to meet the threshold payment
requirement included in 72 P.S. § 10003.1(b).
Petitioner did not report any corporate net income tax on the originally filed return, nor
did Petitioner pay the assessed tax. The instant refund claim is dismissed.
Petitioner’s arguments concerning the filing of the instant refund to preserve claims
outside the bases of assessment are not persuasive because Petitioner never paid the
reported tax and refund cases can only concern monies actually paid to the Commonwealth.
Accordingly, Petitioner’s refund request was correctly dismissed at the Board of Appeals
for lack of jurisdiction.

Conclusion
Petitioner’s request for relief was correctly denied because Petitioner has not provided
sufficient details and evidence in support of its claims. See 72 P.S. § 9705 (imposing the
burden of proof on taxpayers in administrative tax appeals); see also 61 Pa. Code § 701.3(c)
(requiring specific objections supported by legal authority and evidence).
Petitioner has not shown that universal fund receipts, wire maintenance fees, and customer
premise equipment were not derived from providing intrastate telephone messages services. As
these services were related to the transmission of messages, these receipts are properly included in
Petitioner’s taxable gross receipts. See Bell Tel., 348 Pa. at 166 (finding that revenue telephone

satisfactory are part of the charge for transmission of the messages).
